Title: Commentary on the Satipatthana Sutta
Kenneth Chu

7. Introduction
   The Buddha was born as Prince of the ruler of a northern India Kingdom around the 5th
   century BCE. He became aware of the sufferings of the average person when he reached
   adulthood and decided to find solutions to end their sufferings. He left home to study with the
   traditional philosophers (Brahmin) but were not satisfied. He then tried asceticism but found
   that this could not contribute to his objective and such practices were damaging to his health.
   He then sat down below a bodhi tree and meditated. In the course of his meditation, He
   became enlightened with the way to end the sufferings of the sentient beings and start to
   teach his philosophy of the Four Noble Truths and the method of achieving his objective
   called the Noble Eightfold Paths.
   One of the items in the Noble Eightfold Paths is Right Mindfulness (Sati, Satipatthana) which
   is the core of the teachings in the Satipatthana Sutta.
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
8. Outline of the Satipatthana Sutta
   Completed version of the Satipatthana Sutta is available in the Pali Theravada Nikaya text
   number 10. It is also available in Nikaya text number 22, which is slightly longer than the
   number 10 version. The number 22 version is called Maha-satipatthana Sutta (Bhikkhu
   Sujato 2005, 236-237).
   The following outline is based on the number 10 version.
   A) At the town of Kammassadhamma, the Buddha gave the following talk on the Four
   Foundations of Mindfulness to the Sangha.
   i) Buddhist practitioners should dwell in the observation of the body in the body
   ii) Buddhist practitioners should dwell in the observation of the feelings in the feelings
   iii) Buddhist practitioners should dwell in the observation of the mind in the mind
   iv) Buddhist practitioners should dwell in the observation of the object of the mind in the
   object of the mind.
   The above directives are the best way to realize purification, to overcome pain and sorrow,
   and to get ahead on the correct path to enlightenment
   (Thich Nhat Hanh 1990, 3-4).
   B) Instructions for Observation of the Body in the Body
   Buddhist Practitioners should go to a secluded place, sit down cross-legged with upper body
   straight and establish mindfulness. When he breath-in, he is aware he is breathing-in. When
   he breath-out, he is also aware that he is breathing-out. He is aware of the breathing-in and
   breathing-out of a long breath and the same for a short breath. He is also aware that by the
   observation of the breathing of the body in body he can calm the whole body.
   He also observes the body in body externally, or both internally and externally. He observes
   the changes and the details of his body. The practitioner reviews the elements that form the
   body. The elements would include the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and
   the air element.
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
   The observation exercise would enable the Buddhist practitioner to be aware of his actions in
   going, sitting, lying down and any action that he is taking at any particular moment in time.
   In his observation, he contemplated the origination and dissolution of the breath-in body and
   the body itself. The awareness of the impermanency of the body would assist the practitioner
   to generate wisdom and non-attachment to handle greed, hate and delusion (Thich Nhat Hanh
   1990, 4-10).
   C) Instruction for the Observation of Feelings in the Feelings
   The Buddha requested the practitioners to observe and become aware of different types of
   feelings, such as a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling and a neutral feeling. The practitioner
   should also be aware that there are specific areas that these three different types of feelings
   are located, whether it is in the body or based in the mind of the practitioner.
   He should also observe and be aware that whether the three kinds of feelings are generated
   from within or from outside. He should also be aware of the coming-to-be of the feelings and
   the dissolution of the feelings.
   D) Instruction for the Observation of the Mind in the Mind
   The Buddha requested the Buddhist Practitioners to be aware of the following conditions in
   his mind:
   i) Whether his mind is desiring or is not desiring,
   ii) Whether his mind is hating or not hating,
   iii) Whether his mind is in a state of ignorance or not,
   iv) Whether his mind is collected or not,
   v) Whether his mind is distracted or not,
   vi) Whether his mind has a wider scope or a narrow scope,
   vii) Whether his mind is capable of reaching a higher state or not capable,
   viii) Whether his mind is composed or not composed,
   ix) Whether his mind is free or not free.
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
   The practitioner should observe his mind from within or without or both. He should observe
   the arising and the dissolution process of the mind. Such observations should be free and not
   cling to any worldly considerations.
   E) Instructions for the Observation of the Objects of Mind in the Objects of Mind
   The “Object of Mind” is the contents operating in the mind. The contents include all concepts
   and thinking that is in the mind.
   i) Five Hindrances
   These are five mental troubles that would affect the mind to progress on the meditative path:
   (a) Sensual desire, (b) Anger, (c) Dullness and drowsiness, (d) Agitation and remorse, (e)
   Doubt.
   Practitioner should be aware of such objects in mind and overcome the Five Hindrances by
   applying the mindfulness practices.
   ii) Seven Factors of Awakening
   To counter the effect of the Five Hindrances, one can practice the seven factors of
   awakening, which is Mindfulness, Investigation-of-phenomena, Energy, Joy, Ease,
   Concentration and Letting-go.
   The seven factors can help us to stay on our path to enlightenment.
   iii) Five Aggregates of Clinging
   This is the combination of the Five Aggregates with Clinging. An average person, through
   the operation of Five Aggregates created a “self” notion within his mind and caused the
   attachment and mental sufferings.
   The practitioner should be aware that there is no “self” in the Five Aggregates. He should
   exercise non-attachment, understand the impermanency and “non-self” nature of the sentient
   beings.
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
   iv) The Six Sense Organs and the Six Sense Objects
   The six sense organs are our eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.
   The six sense objects are form, sound, smell, taste, object touched, and object of the mind.
   During the observation of the “Objects of the Mind” transmitted through the six sense bases,
   the practitioner should be aware of the impermanent nature of the objects of the mind. He
   should also be aware of the “non-self” nature of the object of the mind. This will allow
   release on the part of the practitioner for greed, hatred and delusion.
   v) Four Noble Truths
   The Four Noble Truths are the core of Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma. He explained to his
   followers the Sufferings, the cause of these Sufferings, the Cessation of these Sufferings, and
   the Path leading to the Cessation of these Sufferings (Noble Eightfold Path).
   The Buddha require the practitioners to observe the object of the mind with regard to the Four
   Noble Truths (Thich Nhat Hanh 1990, 10-19).
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
9. Analysis
   A) Bare Attention and Clear Comprehension
   In his book “The Heart of Buddhist Meditation”, Thera think that there are two concepts one
   need to be aware in the understanding of the Satipatthana Sutta. The first one is Bare
   Attention and the second one is Clear Comprehension. While Bare Attention associates with
   our cognition system, Clear Comprehension associates with the implication of our thoughts
   on the line of action we are going to take.
   i) Bare Attention
   Bare attention is the initial registration of the facts observed by our cognition system before
   the addition of subjective judgement by the observer. After the bare attention stage, the
   observer’s mind will attach the bare attention with personal judgements and store it in the
   memory for future reference and retrieval. By preparing the objects using the process of Bare
   Attention, impurities of prejudice and passion will be excluded from our thoughts before
   putting the matter for examination by our thoughts. This will offer a better chance for the
   practitioner to became aware of the impermanency, suffering and “non-self” nature of our
   existence. Bare Attention only focus in the present, it will not entertain thoughts associated
   with the past and the future. In this way, mind thoughts will not be corrupted by past and
   future actions, which usually are reflections of daydreams. Bare Attention assist the mind to
   focus on positive qualities. It will make the practitioner feel more harmonious and contented
   with the liberation of the mind. Under such circumstances, the practitioner is free from
   Desire, Hatred and Delusion, and can work on his insight to realize the basic characteristics
   of existence: impermanency, suffering and non-self. (Thich Nhat Hanh 1990, 30-44)
   ii) Clear Comprehension
   While the Bare Attention mainly associate with our cognition system of the mind, Clear
   Comprehension is associated with regulation of our on-going activities of our whole body. It
   is the application of the bare mindfulness in the observation and contemplation discussed in
   detail in the Satipatthana Sutta.
   There are four kinds of Clear Comprehension:
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)

* The Clear Comprehension of Purpose
  The practice of Bare Attention provides a mechanism for the practitioner to ‘stop and think’
  as a safeguard on the intend purpose of the proposed mental activities.
* The Clear Comprehension of Suitability
  The practitioners should check whether the selected course of action is in-line with our
  capacities
* The Clear Comprehension of Domain
  There are no specific boundaries as long as the intended activities are within the domain of
  the Dharma.
* The Clear Comprehension of Reality
  It is the awareness of Non-self in our existence (Thera, 1962, 30-56).
  B) Observation of the Body
  The original Discourse included a number of areas for the practice of mindfulness of body,
  but the most representative one is the observation of breathing. The practitioner should
  correctly position oneself in a secluded location and starts to observe its own breath-in and
  breath-out. He should apply the Bare Attention to his breathing at this moment, including the
  length of breathing, depth of breathing and the rhythm of breathing. Calm and happiness will
  naturally result through the attention given to the understanding of the body’s true nature.
  The breaths come and go, the breaths maybe smooth or heavy, the dependency of the body on
  the breath that provide the vital supply of oxygen, all directed to a sense of impermanency,
  suffering and conditioned-arising nature of our body.
  The Clear Comprehension function extends our awareness to various functions of our body,
  such as looking, eating, walking etc. As such the Clear Comprehension will exercise detail
  analysis on the bodily activities and demonstrate and support in our understanding of the
  nature of Reality.
  ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
  C) Observation of Feelings
  Feeling is associated with the reaction from sense inputs. It is where action such as Craving
  and Clinging get its source of supply. If the action of Bare Attention can be applied, the
  initiation of Craving and Clinging can be stopped. The practitioner will not be overwhelmed
  by passionate reaction. As such, suffering will not be initiated. The Satipatthana Sutta offers a
  deterrent to ignoble feeling and keep the practitioner on course in the Path to Enlightenment.
  D) Observation of Mind
  Under the observation of mind in mind, the mind itself is put before the examination of Bare
  Attention. The state of operation in the mind will be categorized as harmful or unharmful,
  whether it is with lust, hatred or delusion, or without such impurities, etc. Such observation of
  the operation of the mind can screen out the unwholesome thought and retain the wholesome
  thoughts, to maintain the mind in a healthy state.
  E) Observation of the Objects in Mind
  The observation of the objects in mind included all thoughts in the practitioner’s spiritual
  world. It is closely related to the mind observation discussed previously. In addition, an
  overall review of the elements affecting the progression of the practitioner on the Path of
  Enlightenment will be involved. This includes the subjects such as the Five hindrances, Five
  Aggregates of Clinging, Four Noble Truths, etc. From the cognition system (Five
  Aggregates), the practitioner understands the impermanency, suffering and “non-self” nature
  of existence. With the help of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, he tackles and overcome
  the effect of the Five Hindrances, and remove the impact of Greed, Hatred and Delusion.
  During the observation of the Objects in Mind, all the previously discussed observation in
  Body, Feeling and Mind seems to be involved at the same time. (Thera 1962, 57-75)
  ![image](data:image/png;base64,)

4. Discussion
   A) Early Buddhism
   In the Noble Eightfold Path, there are two items that are associated with meditation, these are
   Right Concentration and Right Mindfulness. According to Thera, Right Mindfulness is
   definitely required to be practiced by followers to achieve Enlightenment. Satipatthana Sutta
   is the direct instruction taught by the Buddha himself on this subject matter. Although the text
   of the Satipatthana Sutta is passed down from the Theravada document Nikaya, it is used by
   Hinayana and Mahayana Schools alike. This demonstrated the importance of practicing
   mindfulness as part of Buddhist Meditation towards enlightenment. (Thera 1962, 7-15)
   In Thera’s analysis, he maintained that Concentration can be achieved by calming the bodily
   functions such as calming the Breath for the achievement of Absorptions (jhana). Through
   the deepening of Calming, the practitioner can reach Tranquility (Samatha). However, after
   the achievement of Samatha, the mental process connected with Vipassana has to be
   performed to get ahead in the meditation (Thera 1962, 111).
   It is of Y. Karanadasa’s view that while Right Mindfulness carried out the proper analysis of
   our mental activities, it has to be carried out under a properly conditioned mind. Therefore,
   Right Concentration is the definite pre-condition for the cultivation of Wisdom (Karunadasa
   2015, 98).
   However, not all scholars on Early Buddhism agreed on this point. Dr Rahula pointed out in
   his book “What the Buddha Taught” that the development of mental concentration to attain
   one-pointedness of mind (Samatha) existed before the Buddha. Such practice of
   concentration is not fundamentally required for the enlightenment exercise. It is the practice
   of Insight (Vipassana) that lead to the realization of the ultimate Realty and Enlightenment
   (Rahula 1959, 68).
   B) Indian and Tibetan Mahayana Buddhism
   Apart from the guidelines in the Satipatthana Sutta, which is considered as the Theravada
   Teachings, meditative guidelines also existed in the Mahayana Schools of Buddhism. Clear
   directives on meditative procedures are descripted in “The Great Treatise in the Stages of the
   ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
   Path to Enlightenment (Lamrim Chenmo)” written by Ven Tsong Khapa, founder of the
   Gelukpa School of Tibetan Buddhism.
   In this document Ven Tsong Khapa maintained that, to progress on the Path of
   Enlightenment, both form of meditation, that is, Concentration (Samatha) and Insight
   (Vipassana) are required. The practitioner needs Samatha because he has to prepare his mind
   for one-pointed focus, pliancy and serenity. He then continues to apply analysis by wisdom
   (Vipassana) to progress on the road to Enlightenment. How far he can go on this Path
   depends on his capacity and Karma (Culter 2002, 13-26).
   Geshe Lhundue Sopa has the following comment on Tsong Khapa’s document on Samatha
   and Insight:

* Samatha
  Tsong Khapa’s Teachings on the achievement of one-pointed focus originated from ancient
  India. After reaching the state of serenity as required, the practitioner enjoys physical and
  mental bliss (Sopa 2004-2009, 5-7, Vol 4).
* Insight
  With Samatha as pre-condition, the practitioner can proceed to remove mental afflictions
  such as greed, hatred and delusion with cultivated wisdom. The basic problem is a “Self”
  generated by Ignorance. Teachings by Tsong Khapa will help the practitioner to get ahead on
  his Path (Sopa 2004-2009, 1-4, Vol 4).
  Master Luo Shi Xian was an expert on Yogacara School of Buddhism in Hong Kong. In his
  talk on “Core Teachings of Samatha and Vipassana”, he offered three reasons that Buddhist
  followers should practice both Samatha and Vipassana as follows:
  i) Master Luo used the metaphor of someone trying to create a painting. This person
  will need a good sheet of paper and a pen. Samatha is like the sheet of paper and Vipassana is
  the pen to put the paint on the paper. Both the paper and the pen are required to complete the
  work.
  ii) In the learning of Buddhism, there are items that compliment and support each other
  to move ahead on the Path to Enlightenment. Samatha and Vipassana are both part of the
  Noble Eightfold Path and have this complimentary effect.
  iii) In Mahayana Buddhism, practitioners are required to practice Six Paramitas. This
  includes Concentration (Samatha) and Wisdom (Vipassana). Therefore, Mahayana Buddhist
  followers all practice both Samatha and Vipassana together (羅時憲 2017, 36-39).
  ![image](data:image/png;base64,)
  C) Chinese Chan Mahayana Budhism
  In the Platform Sutra of the Six Patriarch, Hui Neng made the following statements:
  i) What is meant by sitting meditation?
  …You detached from “Forms” outwardly, and not disturbed inwardly (Yampolsky 1967,
  140).
  ii) My teaching of the Dharma takes Concentration (Ting, Samatha) and Wisdom (Hui,
  Vipassana) as its base….
  Concentration is the body of Wisdom, and Wisdom is the application (function) of
  Concentration (Yampolsky 1967, 135).
  The Sixth Patriarch proclaimed that Samatha and Vipassana exist together.
  ![image](data:image/png;base64,)

5. Summary
   The Satipatthana Sutta is the record of the Buddha’s personal experience. Through the
   observation of the changes in one’s body and mind, one can come to the awareness of the so
   called “Self” is only delusion created by impermanent events. One should exercise non-
   attachment to it. The practice of the four foundations of mindfulness will help us to
   emancipate from suffering, reduce greed, hatred and delusion and obtain peacefulness of
   mind (陳燕珠 2002, 1).
   From the above Section 4 analysis, we noted that Early Buddhism did not seem to spell out a
   clear relationship between Concentration Meditation (Samatha) and Insight Meditation
   (Vipassana). Mahayana Buddhism in India and Tibet appeared to favour a sequential
   treatment of Samatha and Vipassana, that is, the practitioner use Samatha to achieve one-
   pointed focus first before analyzing the mind by Vipassana.
   In China, Bodhidharma was credited with the initiation of Chan Buddhism and was offered
   the title of the First Patriarch. However, the most important transmission work was carried
   out by the Sixth Patriarch and his Teachings contained in the Platform Sutra. According to
   Hui Neng’s teachings in the Platform Sutra, Concentration Meditation and Insight Meditation
   are of the different facets of the same thing and is practiced together.
   At this juncture, it may be useful to note Ven Vimalarami’s comment in his book “The
   Anapanasati Sutta”. He thinks that the Buddha would definitely not support unilateral belief
   between the dualism of whether the two types of meditations should practice together or
   sequentially. Buddhists should not dogmatically cling on to their views. One should keep
   an open mind in order to understand Buddha’s Teachings (Vimalaramsi 2000, 1-3).
   (Words 3420)
